sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: The 4–11 cm cap is hemispherical at first, then flattens and becomes slightly depressed in the centre. Its color ranges from coppery orange to brick red, sometimes yellow-orange, and fades with age or rain. It may be slightly sticky when young in damp weather, then becomes dry. The fairly close gills change from pale cream to cream-yellow and may turn grey or black along their edges after damage. The white, firm, cylindrical to slightly club-shaped stem greys with age, especially toward the base. The white, brittle flesh first turns reddish when cut, then grey to grey-black; the odor is faint and the taste mild.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This mycorrhizal russula grows on the ground in conifer forests, especially with pines. It is reported from damp sites with acidic, nutrient-poor or chalk-free soils, as well as upland moors. It fruits in summer and autumn.

sections.title: Confusion with the marsh russula
sections.text: Russula paludosa can resemble it in cap color, especially when young. In R. decolorans, the flesh turns grey-black quickly after cutting, particularly in the stem; this reaction helps tell them apart. Reliable identification still depends on the full set of features, not cap color alone.

sections.title: Food safety
sections.text: The DGfM and VAPKO include this species on their edible or recommended mushroom lists. That does not identify a wild specimen: red-capped russulas can resemble one another. Eat a mushroom only when its identity is certain and confirmed by a qualified person.

traits: Cap usually 4–11 cm wide, hemispherical at first, then convex, flattening and becoming slightly depressed; coppery orange to brick red, sometimes yellow-orange, fading with age or rain; slightly sticky when young in damp weather, then dry
Gills fairly close, pale cream then cream-yellow to yellow; their edges may turn grey or black after damage
Stem white, firm, cylindrical to slightly club-shaped, up to about 12 cm; it greys as it ages, especially toward the base
Flesh white and brittle, first turning reddish when cut, then grey to grey-black; odor faint and taste mild
A mycorrhizal russula of conifer forests, especially with pines, including damp sites with acidic or poor soils; fruits in summer and autumn
The coppery cap can resemble the marsh russula (Russula paludosa); in R. decolorans, the flesh turns grey and then black quickly after cutting, especially in the stem, which helps distinguish the two
safetyNote: Edible according to the DGfM and VAPKO lists. Red-capped russulas can be difficult to distinguish, and cap color alone is not enough for a safe identification. Never eat a wild mushroom unless it has been positively identified by a qualified person.
